title: Repeal the 2025 law's Medicaid eligibility cuts
parameters: Repeal the work requirement (sec. 71119), six-month redeterminations for expansion adults (sec. 71107), the retroactive-coverage limit (sec. 71112) and cost sharing for expansion adults (sec. 71120); effective on enactment, before the work requirement's later state start dates bite
eligibility: Medicaid expansion adults and other Medicaid enrollees the 2025 law's eligibility cuts reach; states stop applying the work requirement, six-month redeterminations, the retroactive-coverage limit and expansion-adult cost sharing

vehicle.note: 2029 reconciliation act

current_law: The 2025 law requires community engagement for Medicaid eligibility from the first quarter after December 31, 2026 (sec. 71119) [EV-CAR-001], six-month redeterminations for expansion adults (sec. 71107) [EV-CAR-006], a shorter retroactive-coverage window (sec. 71112) [EV-CAR-007] and cost sharing for expansion adults from October 1, 2028 (sec. 71120) [EV-CAR-010].
cost_source: part 2 (restoration, FY2030)

title: Restore lawfully present immigrants to Medicaid and the premium credit
parameters: Repeal secs. 71109 and 71301's limits and the emergency-Medicaid match cut (sec. 71110); people without status are the immigration flagship's decision (point 3)
eligibility: Lawfully present immigrants, who regain Medicaid and the premium credit; people without status are left to the immigration flagship (point 3)

vehicle.note: 2029 reconciliation act

current_law: The 2025 law bars federal Medicaid payment for many lawfully present immigrants from October 1, 2026 (sec. 71109) and caps the emergency-Medicaid match at the state's regular rate (sec. 71110) [EV-CAR-008, EV-CAR-009]; sec. 71301 limits the premium credit to certain immigrants [EV-CAR-016].
cost_source: part 2 (restoration, FY2030)

title: Restore Medicaid financing: provider taxes and state directed payments
parameters: Repeal secs. 71115 and 71116 and the expansion-incentive limit (sec. 71114); lasts until each state's Medicaid enrollees join the plan (HLT-7.03)
eligibility: States and their providers; federal Medicaid financing is restored for each state until its Medicaid enrollees join the plan

vehicle.note: 2029 reconciliation act

current_law: The 2025 law limits provider taxes (sec. 71115) and caps state directed payments (sec. 71116) [EV-CAR-011, EV-CAR-012], and limits the expansion incentive to states that expanded before January 1, 2026 (sec. 71114) [EV-CAR-013].
cost_source: part 2 (restoration, FY2030)

title: Restore the enhanced premium credits and repeal the marketplace verification rules until wave 1
parameters: Enhanced credit schedule for plan year 2030; repeal secs. 71303 and 71304 (verification before credits; special-enrollment limits); the individual market joins the plan on January 1, 2031, which ends the credits
eligibility: People who buy marketplace coverage and receive the enhanced premium credit, for plan year 2030 only; the individual market joins the plan on January 1, 2031, which ends the credits

vehicle.note: 2029 reconciliation act

current_law: The enhanced premium credits expired [EV-CAR-028]; the 2025 law withholds the credit until the Exchange verifies eligibility (sec. 71303) and denies it for income-based special enrollment (sec. 71304) [EV-CAR-017, EV-CAR-018].
cost_source: part 2 (restoration, FY2030)

title: Medicare Advantage: fix coding and benchmarks on MedPAC's method
parameters: Risk scores from two years of encounter data with a coding-intensity adjustment set to MedPAC's estimate; benchmarks rebased so Advantage pays no more than traditional Medicare for similar people; payment year 2030 at half strength, 2031 in full; savings counted at MedPAC's lower 2026 estimate (14%, about $76 billion in 2026); Advantage ends at the endpoint (HLT-7.25)
eligibility: Medicare Advantage plans (their payment is reduced to traditional Medicare's level for similar people); Medicare Advantage enrollees keep their coverage until Advantage ends at the endpoint

vehicle.note: 2029 reconciliation act

current_law: Medicare Advantage spending runs above traditional Medicare's for similar people [EV-CAR-061]; MedPAC estimates 14%, about $76 billion, more in 2026 [EV-CAR-135]. Current law does not adjust benchmarks or coding on MedPAC's method.
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 2 (Advantage fix savings)

title: Drug price negotiation extended to all drugs Medicare covers, then to the plan
parameters: Builds on the 2022 law's Medicare negotiation; removes its yearly drug count and small-molecule wait; negotiated prices apply to the plan from 2031 (HLT-7.13)
eligibility: Everyone who takes drugs Medicare covers; from 2031 the plan's enrollees; the manufacturers whose prices are negotiated pay through lower prices

vehicle.note: 2029 reconciliation act

current_law: The 2022 law lets Medicare negotiate prices for a limited number of drugs a year, with a wait for small-molecule drugs; this extends it to all drugs Medicare covers.
cost_source: 6-cost.md, inside the plan's cost (the model's drug price cut)

title: Rural health through USDA Rural Development: scale what exists
parameters: Community Facilities direct lending for rural hospitals, clinics and nursing homes raised to $3-5 billion a year; $200-500 million a year of competitive grants restored; Rural Development's state offices as a front door to HRSA, CMS and the Rural Health Transformation Program; no new service. The navigator's remit is set in section 5
eligibility: Rural hospitals, clinics and nursing homes, and their communities, through Rural Development lending and competitive grants; no new service

vehicle.note: 2029 reconciliation act

current_law: Rural Development's Community Facilities lending and competitive grants exist today; the 2025 law adds a separate Rural Health Transformation Program [EV-CAR-015]. This scales the existing USDA programs without a new service.
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 2 (USDA lending and grants)

title: Entitlement: every resident
parameters: Every person who lives in the United States is entitled to the plan once their wave starts; residency by rule, on the S. 1506 model (sec. 102), which the immigration flagship receives as the proposal for shared rule 3; people without status: the immigration flagship decides (open for that owner)
eligibility: Every person who lives in the United States, once their wave starts; people without status are decided by the immigration flagship

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: New. Medicare, Medicaid and the marketplaces cover people by age, income or category; no program entitles every resident.
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (the plan on the coverage model)

title: Automatic enrollment and renewal from records; no premiums; a card without a Social Security number
status: decided (DEC-2026-11-10-09); the card adopted from the S. 1506 comparison (follows from DEC-2026-11-10-09)
parameters: Enrolled at birth, on establishing residency, or on the group's wave date, from records the government holds (tax, Social Security, Medicaid, employer payroll); renewal at most yearly and without forms where records suffice; no work requirement; no premium; the card shows no Social Security number (S. 1506 sec. 105); anyone missed is enrolled at the point of care
eligibility: Every person entitled to the plan; no premium, no work requirement; anyone missed is enrolled at the point of care

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: New. Medicaid and the marketplaces require applications and renewals; removing auto-enrollment cut enrollment by a third in one state's exchange [EV-CAR-206], and many Medicaid disenrollments were for paperwork [EV-CAR-210].
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (the plan on the coverage model)

title: The waves and the endpoint, written as automatic
parameters: Wave 1, January 1, 2031: the uninsured, the individual market and every child under 19, plus Medicare at 60 (HLT-2.04). Wave 2, 2033-35: Medicaid and CHIP enrollees and employer groups together, required, in three cohorts on January 1 of 2033, 2034 and 2035 (working choice: about a third of each group a year; Medicaid by state, employer groups by firm size, smallest firms first). Endpoint, January 1, 2035: everyone else, including today's Medicare enrollees, FEHB enrollees and any group not yet moved. Each date takes effect unless Congress votes to delay it; HHS publishes a readiness report within nine months of enactment for wave 1 and 18 months before each later date (a published count, not a gate)
eligibility: Wave 1: the uninsured, the individual market, every child under 19 and people 60 to 64 (HLT-2.04); wave 2: Medicaid and CHIP enrollees and employer groups in three cohorts; endpoint: everyone else, including Medicare and FEHB enrollees

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

agency: HHS (CMS); Labor and Treasury for employer cohorts
current_law: New. Coverage now depends on the payer: Medicaid, employer plans, the individual market and Medicare each start and end on their own rules.
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (the plan on the coverage model)

title: No gap in anyone's coverage
parameters: A person leaves their old coverage only when the plan is active for them; an employer or state may not end coverage before its cohort's date; anyone who loses coverage before their wave is enrolled in the plan at once
eligibility: Everyone entering the plan; people who lose coverage before their wave; employers and states are barred from ending coverage early

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: New. Current law has no guarantee that a person leaves old coverage only when new coverage is active; unwinding showed many people lost Medicaid for procedural reasons [EV-CAR-210].
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (the plan on the coverage model)

title: The territories
status: decided in substance (point 3, DEC-2026-11-10-09: every resident); the wave and the share are working choices
parameters: Residents of Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, the Northern Mariana Islands and American Samoa are residents under HLT-7.01 and are entitled on the same dates: the uninsured, the individual market and children in wave 1 (2031); Medicaid enrollees in wave 2's first cohort (2033, working choice: their programs are the smallest and run on capped allotments); employer groups by firm size with the rest of wave 2; Medicare enrollees at the endpoint. Each territory pays the fund the same share as a state under HLT-7.17 (half of its own current Medicaid spending for the people who move), which is small because federal Medicaid money there is capped; the cap and the territories' separate matching rate end for the care that moves
eligibility: Residents of Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, the Northern Mariana Islands and American Samoa (about 3.5 million people)

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: Territories' federal Medicaid money is capped by an annual allotment, with the territory paying all costs above it; the statutory matching rate is 55%, with higher rates set by recent laws (83% for four territories; 76% for Puerto Rico through FY2027) [EV-CAR-358] [EV-CAR-359]; Puerto Rico's rate reverts to 55% and its cap is cut from FY2028 under current law [EV-CAR-362].
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 2 (the territories, about $0.13 trillion over FY2030-39)

title: Comprehensive benefits, including abortion and reproductive care
parameters: Hospital, outpatient, primary and preventive care, prescription drugs, mental health and addiction treatment, maternity and newborn care, comprehensive reproductive care including abortion, contraception and fertility care, dental, vision and hearing, rehabilitation and devices, laboratory and imaging; the S. 1506 list (sec. 201) as the drafting base, without its long-term care title (HLT-7.07)
eligibility: Every person enrolled in the plan

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: New. Medicare, Medicaid and private plans each cover different benefit lists; the Hyde limits keep federal programs from covering most abortion care (RTS-2).
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (the plan on the coverage model)

title: Small capped copays above 200% of poverty
parameters: No cost sharing below 200% of the poverty guideline, or for anyone for primary care, prevention, maternity, mental health and chronic-condition drugs; small fixed copays for other services above that line; a yearly cap of $1,000 a person (working figure); income from the prior year's tax records, and no copay where no record shows income above the line; no deductibles, coinsurance or networks. S. 1506's stricter protection (no cost sharing at or below 250%) is noted as the alternative
eligibility: Enrollees above 200% of the poverty guideline pay the small copays; no cost sharing below that line or for the listed services

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: New. Traditional Medicare has deductibles and coinsurance; many workers face deductibles [EV-CAR-113]. The plan replaces them with small fixed copays above 200% of poverty.
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (the plan on the coverage model)

title: Long-term care left to part B; Medicaid's long-term care continues meanwhile
parameters: Home and community services and nursing-home care stay in Medicaid, with today's eligibility and state roles, when Medicaid enrollees' other care moves to the plan; part B decides whether and how they move; estate recovery is a part B question
eligibility: Medicaid enrollees who use long-term care; today's eligibility and state roles continue

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: Medicaid pays for most long-term care today, with state roles and waiting lists for home and community services [EV-CAR-138]; this keeps that arrangement meanwhile.
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (the plan on the coverage model)

title: Participation, no balance billing, all-in or all-out private contracts, no utilization bonuses
status: adopted from the S. 1506 comparison (follows from DEC-2026-11-10-09)
parameters: A participating provider accepts the plan's payment in full; a provider who contracts privately for covered services does so for all patients for a year, as Medicare's opt-out works today; no pay or bonus tied to the volume of care used; the VA, IHS, tribal and military facilities qualify as providers (S. 1506 secs. 301-303, 302(b))
eligibility: Every provider that takes part in the plan, and the patients they treat; VA, IHS, tribal and military facilities qualify as providers

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: Medicare's opt-out lets a provider contract privately for a period; providers may accept or refuse Medicare and Medicaid patients, and Medicaid may bar balance billing. This adds one participation rule.
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (the plan on the coverage model)

title: Non-discrimination, with a private right of action
status: adopted from the S. 1506 comparison (follows from DEC-2026-11-10-09)
parameters: No provider or the plan may discriminate on the grounds in S. 1506 sec. 104; a person may sue to enforce it
eligibility: Everyone seeking care from a provider in the plan; any person may sue to enforce it

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: New. Existing law bars discrimination in federally funded health programs in part, enforced mainly by the Office for Civil Rights; the plan adds a private right of action.
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (the plan on the coverage model)

title: Hospital rates on a five-year glide path to about 1.15 times Medicare
parameters: In 2031 the plan's hospital conversion factor pays, on average, today's all-payer average hospital rate (about 1.25 times Medicare on the coverage model's inputs; project arithmetic); it falls in five equal steps to about 1.15 times Medicare in 2036; the target by service is set by rule (working figure 1.15)
eligibility: Hospitals paid by the plan; the plan (the fund) pays the rates

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: Employers and private insurers pay hospitals far more than Medicare does, 254 percent of Medicare on average in 2022 [EV-CAR-131]; Medicare and Medicaid pay set rates. The plan adopts one rate path.
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (the plan on the coverage model)

title: Global budgets for rural, critical-access and safety-net hospitals
parameters: A fixed yearly budget, set from the hospital's prior net patient revenue and indexed, with a volume corridor, on Maryland's model; eligible: critical-access and sole-community hospitals, hospitals in areas under the plan's rural test (the housing dossier's one rural test, up to 35,000 people, `DEC-2026-11-10-02`), and safety-net hospitals (top quarter by share of Medicaid and uninsured patient days); during and after the glide. Scale: about 2,176 of 4,306 acute-care hospitals were rural in a 2020 count, 1,334 of them critical access (Sheps Center, 2020), and MedPAC counted about 1,370 critical access hospitals in FY2024
eligibility: Critical-access and sole-community hospitals, hospitals in areas under the plan's rural test, and safety-net hospitals (top quarter by share of Medicaid and uninsured patient days)

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: Hospitals are paid by service; Maryland's global-budget model is the only all-payer example [EV-CAR-259].
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (the plan on the coverage model)

title: Physicians and other clinicians at Medicare's fee schedule, with primary-care and rural add-ons
parameters: Medicare's fee schedule from 2031; a primary-care add-on and a rural and shortage-area add-on (working figure: 10% each, on Medicare's shortage-area bonus); no glide
eligibility: Physicians and other clinicians who take part in the plan, with add-ons for primary care and for rural and shortage areas

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: Medicare pays physicians on its fee schedule; Medicaid and private plans pay by their own rates. The plan uses Medicare's schedule with two add-ons.
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (the plan on the coverage model)

title: Drug prices: negotiated for all drugs, a fallback price, a formulary
status: decided (DEC-2026-11-10-09); the fallback and formulary adopted from the S. 1506 comparison (follows from DEC-2026-11-10-09)
parameters: Annual negotiation for every covered drug (HLT-6.02); if no agreement is reached, the price is the lowest of the VA's price and Medicaid's best price (the fallback in S. 1506 sec. 1012(d)); a national formulary that favors generics and biosimilars
eligibility: Drug manufacturers (negotiated prices) and everyone who takes covered drugs

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: Medicare negotiates prices for a limited set of drugs (HLT-6.02); there is no national formulary or fallback price.
cost_source: 6-cost.md, inside the plan's cost (the model's drug price cut)

title: Medicare Advantage ends at the endpoint
status: follows from memo 1 B (DEC-2026-11-10-09) and HLT-7.23 (DEC-2026-11-10-12)
parameters: No new Advantage contracts after plan year 2034; the plan pays providers directly from January 1, 2035
eligibility: Medicare Advantage plans and their enrollees, who move to the plan at the endpoint

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: Medicare Advantage plans run today under contracts with CMS and cover most of Part A and B spending [EV-CAR-061].
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (the plan on the coverage model)

title: Hospital transition fund and a revenue floor for global-budget hospitals
parameters: A capped fund, $100 billion over FY2033-38 (working figure, range $50-150 billion), for hospitals whose net patient revenue falls more than 5% below their pre-transition level as their patients' coverage moves; first claim for global-budget hospitals (HLT-7.11) and sole providers in their area; for three years after their area moves, global budgets are at least the hospital's pre-transition net patient revenue, indexed, paid from the fund; replacement falls from 100% of the loss in the first year to 20% in the fifth; conditions: keep emergency, obstetric and behavioral health services open, no fund money for executive bonuses or distributions to owners. Keeps the five-year glide unchanged
eligibility: Hospitals whose net patient revenue falls more than 5% below their pre-transition level as their patients' coverage moves; global-budget hospitals and sole providers in their area have first claim; the federal government pays the fund

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: New. No federal fund supports hospitals whose revenue falls as coverage moves.
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 2 (firm, about $0.10 trillion over FY2033-38) and part 3 (hospital options)

title: Help for insurance and billing workers
parameters: Wage replacement and continued pay toward retirement for up to three years, training, job placement, and first claim on the plan's administrative jobs; eligibility from employer records (an insurer, billing firm or provider billing office certifies the layoff), not individual proof; FY2033-38
eligibility: Insurance and billing workers laid off because of the plan, certified by the employer (an insurer, billing firm or provider billing office); not individual proof

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: New. Trade adjustment assistance and unemployment insurance help displaced workers generally; no program is built for insurance and billing workers (whether trade adjustment was reauthorized after 2021 is still to be checked).
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 2 (worker help)

title: States keep paying a share: maintenance of effort
status: decided (DEC-2026-11-10-09); the mechanism, a direct obligation on the Part D clawback model, is a drafting and legal choice that follows from it
parameters: Amount: each state pays the fund, monthly, half of its own current Medicaid spending for its residents who move (working figure; range 0-80%, set by the financing settlement), indexed to the plan's per-person cost growth; a state's spending on dual eligibles' Medicare premiums and cost sharing, which end at the endpoint, counts in that spending; long-term care stays with the state under HLT-7.07. Mechanism (one, used in every section): a direct obligation written in the Act, on the model of Medicare Part D's "phased-down state contribution" (the clawback) that states have paid since 2006 (42 U.S.C. 1396u-5(c)). It is not a condition on Medicaid or on any grant: a state owes it whether or not it keeps a Medicaid program, and it is collected by offset against federal payments to the state, with interest, as the clawback is. Legal risk, stated: the Supreme Court held in 2012 that threatening states' existing Medicaid funds to force a new program was coercive (*NFIB v. Sebelius*); the clawback is a different instrument (an obligation, not a condition) and has never been decided on the merits, so a court could still read the offset as the same leverage. If it fails in court, the payment ends (hold harmless) and the financing settlement covers the difference, about $307 billion in 2032 (section 6, part 6). When part B decides long-term care, if it brings new federal money for states' long-term care, the payment moves to become a condition on that new money, which a state may decline, and the offset ends
eligibility: States pay: each state pays the fund a fixed amount for its residents who move

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2): a direct obligation of states, collected by offset; offsetting receipts in the booking

current_law: States pay about a third of Medicaid's cost [EV-CAR-060]. Since 2006 states have paid Medicare Part D a monthly phased-down contribution for dual eligibles' drugs, collected with interest by offset against federal Medicaid payments (42 U.S.C. 1396u-5(c)) [EV-CAR-353] [EV-CAR-354]. NFIB v. Sebelius (2012) held that threatening existing Medicaid funds to force a new program was coercive [EV-CAR-351].
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 4 (the fund's streams)

title: Employers' transitional contribution, required
parameters: From the date an employer's workers or their children move until the financing settlement's payroll contribution takes effect, the employer pays the fund a set share of what it paid toward premiums for that coverage in a base year (2030), indexed to the plan's per-person cost growth; paid with payroll tax deposits; an employer that offered no coverage pays nothing; the share is the financing settlement's (working figure: about 65%, the share at which employer moves cost the federal budget nothing on the coverage model; project arithmetic)
eligibility: Employers pay: those whose workers or their children move to the plan; an employer that offered no coverage pays nothing

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: New. Employers now buy coverage for their workers; the cost is excluded from workers' taxable pay.
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 4 (the fund's streams)

title: The administering agency
parameters: CMS runs the plan, with Medicare's contractors and claims systems; its staffing, regional structure and the readiness reports are in section 5
eligibility: The plan's enrollees, served through CMS and Medicare's contractors

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: CMS runs Medicare through its contractors and claims systems; this extends that machinery to the plan [EV-CAR-310].
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (the plan on the coverage model)

title: A Beneficiary Ombudsman
status: adopted from the S. 1506 comparison (follows from DEC-2026-11-10-09)
parameters: Handles complaints and appeals and reports yearly; may not advocate for higher payments (S. 1506 title IV)
eligibility: The plan's enrollees, who use the Ombudsman for complaints and appeals

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: Medicare has had a Medicare Beneficiary Ombudsman within CMS since the 2003 Medicare law; the plan's Ombudsman extends the role to every enrollee, on S. 1506's terms [EV-CAR-280].
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (the plan on the coverage model)

title: An Office of Health Equity, an Office of Primary Health Care and a data firewall
status: adopted from the S. 1506 comparison (follows from DEC-2026-11-10-09)
parameters: Both offices as in S. 1506 secs. 616-617, the primary-care office setting national goals within a year; plan and equity data may not be used for any law enforcement or immigration purpose (its immigration side goes to the immigration flagship with point 3)
eligibility: The plan's enrollees and the public; the data firewall protects people whose data the plan holds

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: New. No federal Office of Health Equity or Office of Primary Health Care of this kind exists in law, and no data firewall covers health data for immigration use [EV-CAR-286].
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (the plan on the coverage model)

title: One trust fund with named streams
parameters: Receives: Medicare's payroll tax and general revenue for Parts B and D (premiums end for each group as it moves); the federal Medicaid and CHIP money and premium-credit money the plan replaces; FEHB's employer share, which is the contribution the government pays for its own workers under HLT-7.26 (intragovernmental, counted once and not as revenue); the revenue from ending the employer tax exclusion, counted only on former premiums that become taxable wages, never on premiums replaced by the employer contribution; the states' payments (HLT-7.17); the employer contribution (HLT-7.18); new revenue from the financing settlement. The hospital insurance trust fund is kept whole until the endpoint, with Medicare savings credited to it first, then folds in
eligibility: Pays for the plan from its named streams: Medicare's payroll tax and general revenue, federal Medicaid, CHIP and premium-credit money, FEHB's employer share, revenue from ending the employer tax exclusion, state payments, the employer contribution and new financing revenue

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: Medicare, Medicaid and the premium credits are paid from separate trust funds and appropriations [EV-CAR-052]; this brings them into one fund.
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 4 (the fund's streams)

title: No duplicative private coverage from the endpoint; supplemental coverage allowed
parameters: From January 1, 2035 no one may sell or offer coverage that duplicates the plan's benefits, as in Canada and S. 1506 (secs. 107, 801-802), rather than parallel private insurance as in the UK and Australia; coverage of benefits the plan does not cover stays legal; COBRA ends then. Before then, private and employer coverage continue for groups not yet moved. Private firms may serve as the plan's claims contractors. The rule meets the McCarran-Ferguson Act's test, that a federal law displaces state insurance law only if it "specifically relates to the business of insurance" (15 U.S.C. 1012(b)), because it regulates who may sell health coverage; a statement in the Act saying so supports the drafting, and the legal review stays at L4
eligibility: Insurers and employers, who may not sell or offer duplicative coverage from the endpoint; anyone may still buy coverage of benefits the plan does not cover

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: Employers and insurers may offer coverage that duplicates one another; COBRA continues coverage after job loss [EV-CAR-275].
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (the plan on the coverage model)

title: The VA, TRICARE and the Indian Health Service continue, and the people they serve are also entitled to the plan
parameters: Eligibility for VA care, TRICARE and the IHS is unchanged; their facilities are plan providers, and the plan pays IHS and tribal facilities at its rates for the plan's enrollees, as Medicaid and Medicare do now; no change to the IHS without consultation with tribal leaders (S. 1506 sec. 901(c)). Open: how the IHS is funded alongside the plan, including whether advance appropriations continue; whether TRICARE's purchased care folds into the plan (the House bill's choice) or continues
eligibility: People served by the VA, TRICARE and the Indian Health Service, who keep that eligibility and are also entitled to the plan; IHS and tribal facilities are paid at the plan's rates

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: The VA, TRICARE and the IHS are separate federal programs with their own eligibility [EV-CAR-315]; the IHS is funded by annual and advance appropriations [EV-CAR-348]. This keeps them and adds plan entitlement.
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (the plan on the coverage model)

title: Today's Medicare moves into the plan at the endpoint
parameters: Parts A, B and D, Advantage and Medigap end for covered services on January 1, 2035; enrollees get the plan's benefit and copay rules (HLT-7.05, 7.06); Part B and D premiums end then
eligibility: Today's Medicare enrollees, who move into the plan at the endpoint

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: Medicare Parts A, B and D, Advantage and Medigap run as separate coverage today; the plan replaces them at the endpoint [EV-CAR-288].
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (the plan on the coverage model)

title: FEHB folds in at the endpoint
parameters: Federal employees and retirees join the plan with the endpoint cohort; the federal government pays the employer contribution (HLT-7.18) for them like any employer, the same money as HLT-7.22's FEHB employer share (an intragovernmental transfer, not revenue)
eligibility: Federal employees and retirees (FEHB enrollees), who join with the endpoint cohort; the federal government pays the employer contribution for them

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: FEHB covers federal employees and retirees through private plans, with the government paying an employer share [EV-CAR-315].
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (the plan on the coverage model)

title: Ownership stays as it is, with targeted guardrails
parameters: No public takeover of hospitals or clinics. Guardrails: ownership transparency (every owner of a participating provider reported to CMS and published); limits on private-equity buyouts of hospitals, nursing homes and physician practices (working choice: prior notice and review of any such acquisition, with authority to block one that would reduce access or quality); regional review of large capital projects so new money goes where care is short (working choice: projects above a threshold set by rule). Not adopted: S. 1506's bar on profit from the plan's payments and its public capital budget for every hospital.
eligibility: Owners and acquirers of participating hospitals, nursing homes and physician practices; sponsors of large capital projects

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

agency: HHS (CMS); FTC and Justice for acquisitions
current_law: Medicare collects some ownership data on enrolled providers; acquisitions are reviewed only under general antitrust law; no federal review of capital projects. Commercial prices rise with provider market power [EV-CAR-340].
cost_source: 6-cost.md: no material federal cost (administration inside the plan's 5%)

title: The legacy upgrades from 2031
parameters: A $5,000 yearly out-of-pocket cap in traditional Medicare and hearing and vision coverage from January 1, 2031; dental phased in from 2033; the plan's benefit replaces them in 2035
eligibility: Today's Medicare enrollees in traditional Medicare, until the plan's benefit replaces the upgrades in 2035

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: Traditional Medicare has no yearly limit on out-of-pocket spending for Parts A and B, while Medicare Advantage plans must cap costs [EV-CAR-137]; hearing, vision and most dental care are not covered.
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 2 (Medicare upgrades, FY2031-34)

title: Guaranteed issue of Medigap, 2031-34
status: adopted from the S. 1506 comparison (follows from DEC-2026-11-10-09)
parameters: Any Medicare enrollee may buy any Medigap plan at any time without medical underwriting (S. 1506 sec. 1005)
eligibility: Any Medicare enrollee, who may buy any Medigap plan without medical underwriting; Medigap insurers must sell to them

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: Medigap insurers may underwrite medically outside a person's first enrollment window in most states.
cost_source: no federal cost

title: No 24-month wait for people on disability
status: adopted from the S. 1506 comparison (follows from DEC-2026-11-10-09)
parameters: From January 1, 2031, people awarded Social Security disability benefits are entitled to Medicare at once (S. 1506 sec. 1004)
eligibility: People awarded Social Security disability benefits, who become entitled to Medicare at once

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: People awarded Social Security disability benefits wait 24 months before Medicare coverage starts [EV-CAR-342, EV-CAR-343].
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 2 (disability wait)

title: Medicare at 60
parameters: From January 1, 2031, people 60 to 64 are entitled to Medicare with the upgrades; those uninsured or in the individual market are enrolled in the plan instead; those with employer coverage may choose Medicare as primary, with their employer paying the transitional contribution (HLT-7.18)
eligibility: People 60 to 64: those uninsured or in the individual market are enrolled in the plan; those with employer coverage may choose Medicare as primary, with the employer paying the transitional contribution

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: Medicare eligibility starts at 65, with exceptions for disability and end-stage renal disease; people 60 to 64 are not eligible.
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 1 (Medicare at 60 in the model's staged path)

title: No abortion funding limit on the plan's fund
parameters: The plan pays for abortion like any covered service, notwithstanding any appropriations limit (as S. 1506 sec. 701(b)(3) does for its fund)
eligibility: Everyone enrolled in the plan who needs abortion care

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)

current_law: The Hyde limits keep federal funds from paying for abortion in most programs, set by annual appropriations riders [EV-CAR-330, EV-CAR-331].
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 2 (small; inside the plan's cost)

title: End the Hyde Amendment and the other federal abortion funding limits
parameters: Repeal the statutory limits (for Defense health care, 10 U.S.C. 1093; the statutory cross-reference that applies Hyde to the IHS; CHIP's own limits; the ACA's segregation rule, 42 U.S.C. 18023) and override the annual appropriations riders (the Labor-HHS Hyde sections 506 and 507, FEHB's sections 613 and 614, D.C.'s section 810, the Peace Corps proviso, and the Department of Justice limit that reaches federal prisoners) by a "notwithstanding" clause in the 2029 Act; the plan's appropriations acts carry none. Scope of "in general" (`DEC-2026-11-10-11`, extended by `DEC-2026-11-11-01`), working reading: every federal limit on paying for abortion in domestic programs, federal custody and federal service (the Peace Corps), which also brings in Title X's section 1008 (42 U.S.C. 300a-6). Foreign assistance is in scope (`DEC-2026-11-11-01`): repeal the Helms amendment (Foreign Assistance Act sec. 104(f)(1), 22 U.S.C. 2151b(f)(1)) and the abortion clause of sec. 104(f)(3) (research on abortion as a method of family planning), and override their yearly restatements in the State-Foreign Operations act (in the FY2026 act, Division F, sec. 7018's abortion clauses and sec. 7057(d)(2)'s condition that UNFPA not fund abortions) by the same "notwithstanding" clause; the bars on involuntary sterilization stay. This dossier holds foreign assistance until a dossier owns it. Federal conscience laws are unchanged here (the rights dossier owns them with RTS-1)
eligibility: People covered by federal programs with abortion funding limits: Defense health care, the IHS, CHIP, ACA plans, FEHB, D.C. and the State-Foreign Operations programs

vehicle.note: Medicare for All Act of 2029 (regular order under D2)
plan-era appropriations acts carry no Hyde-type riders

agency: HHS; OPM; Defense; VA; Justice; State
current_law: The Labor-HHS act bars funds for abortion (sec. 506) with exceptions (sec. 507); FEHB (secs. 613-614), D.C. (sec. 810), State-Foreign Operations funds, Defense (10 U.S.C. 1093), the IHS (by cross-reference) and CHIP (its own statute) have their own limits [EV-CAR-330, EV-CAR-331, EV-CAR-332]; the ACA segregates abortion funds (42 U.S.C. 18023). The Foreign Assistance Act bars part I funds from paying for abortion as a method of family planning (sec. 104(f), the Helms amendment) [EV-CAR-369], and the FY2026 State-Foreign Operations act restates it (sec. 7018) and conditions UNFPA funds on UNFPA not funding abortions (sec. 7057(d)(2)) [EV-CAR-374, EV-CAR-375].
cost_source: 6-cost.md, part 2 (small; inside the plan's cost)
